red_flags.text: Arterial insufficiency: pale, cool, slow or absent capillary refill, loss of the Doppler signal, and no bleeding on pinprick.
Venous congestion: blue or purple, swollen and tense, very brisk capillary refill, and dark blood on pinprick.
A swelling at the pedicle or under the flap: haematoma compressing the vessels.
A change in an implantable Doppler or tissue oximetry trend.
Hypotension, hypothermia, hypovolaemia or vasoconstrictor use in a patient with a fresh free flap.

do_now.text: Inform the operating plastic surgeon immediately on any change. Salvage rates fall the later compromise is recognised, so the call is never premature.
Return a compromised free flap to theatre for exploration promptly rather than observing it.
At the bedside, release tight dressings, ties, tracheostomy tapes and sutures, and correct any position that kinks or compresses the pedicle.

assess.text: Colour, capillary refill, temperature, turgor, Doppler signal and pinprick bleeding, compared each time with the last recorded observation.
Monitor frequently in the first 24 to 48 hours, when most pedicle thromboses occur; follow the unit's documented schedule.
Distinguish arterial from venous problems: management and urgency differ.
Pedicled flaps fail mainly at the tip, and mostly from venous congestion or tension; free flaps fail all at once.

investigate.text: Handheld or implantable Doppler, used by someone who has heard this flap's normal signal.
Haemoglobin and coagulation if a haematoma is suspected.
No investigation should delay a return to theatre for a clinically failing free flap.

resuscitate.text: Keep the patient warm, well filled and normotensive, with good analgesia. Flap perfusion follows systemic perfusion.

definitive.text: Re-explore early: evacuate haematoma, inspect the pedicle for kinking, twisting or compression, and revise a thrombosed anastomosis.
Most pedicle thromboses declare within the first days after surgery, which is when monitoring must be most intensive.
Venous congestion with no surgically correctable cause: consider medicinal leeches as salvage.
Patients treated with leeches need antibiotic prophylaxis active against Aeromonas, per local microbiology advice.
Late or partial flap loss: debride dead tissue and plan secondary cover rather than waiting for demarcation to cause infection.

escalate.text: Any concern about a free flap at night is a consultant phone call, not a morning ward-round item.
Theatre should treat a returning free flap as an emergency category, agreed in advance.
Discuss blood pressure targets and vasoactive drugs with the anaesthetic and critical care teams before giving them.

notes: Venous problems are commoner than arterial ones and present more slowly. A flap that is a little darker on each check is failing.
Ask the nurse what they think. The person who has looked at the flap every hour is the best monitor available.
Write the expected normal for this flap in the notes: colour, refill and where the Doppler signal is found.
